en: The Compendium of the Perfections.
1. The Compendium of the Perfection of Giving.
Homage to the Buddha!

One who desires to ascend to the state of the Tathāgatas, relying with reverence upon the Three Jewels and fixing the mind unwaveringly on enlightenment, should first practice the exchange of self and others.
Thereafter, one intent on the welfare of the world should apply oneself to the practice of giving in such a way that,
even when asked for one's own limbs, there may be no deformity caused by the contraction of one's yoga.

A bodhisattva ought to abandon that very affliction which consists in the guise of acquisition—that which would lead to the accumulation of the fault of stinginess or prevent the cultivation of the mind of renunciation. (1.3)

How, then, could a bodhisattva take up a jewel, wealth, or even sovereignty over heaven, when that which is skilled in opposing the intention to renounce creates an obstacle to the path of perfect enlightenment? (Ps 1.4)

Recalling the supreme conduct of the Munis as well as his own vow directed toward that same goal, he should cultivate these right reflections in his mind for the sake of subduing attachment to possessions: Ps_1.5: "I have entered this forest out of fear of the world; having abandoned my kin, I have come here alone. What need have I for a wife? She would be a source of bondage. Ps_1.6: "I have renounced all property and am now without possessions; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of suffering. Ps_1.7: "I have cast off all worldly affairs and dwell in solitude; what use have I for a wife? She would be a cause of distraction. Ps_1.8: "I have transcended all attachments and am free from desire; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of passion. Ps_1.9: "I have abandoned all objects of sense and abide in peace; what use have I for a wife? She would be a cause of agitation. Ps_1.10: "I have relinquished all forms of existence and am intent on liberation; what use have I for a wife? She would be a bond of rebirth. Ps_1.11: "I have severed the ties of affection and am without longing; what use have I for a wife? She would be a snare of craving. Ps_1.12: "I have destroyed the arrows of Māra and am invincible; what use have I for a wife? She would be a weapon of the Evil One. Ps_1.13: "I have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra and reached the further shore; what use have I for a wife? She would be a whirlpool of the flood. Ps_1.14: "I have attained the state of a sage and am beyond reproach; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of blame. Ps_1.15: "I have realized the noble truths and am established in the Dharma; what use have I for a wife? She would be a hindrance to the path. Ps_1.16: "I have attained the fruit of the holy life and am free from defilement; what use have I for a wife? She would be a stain upon purity. Ps_1.17: "I have conquered all enemies and am without fear; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of terror. Ps_1.18: "I have attained the bliss of tranquility and am cooled by peace; what use have I for a wife? She would be a fire of burning passion. Ps_1.19: "I have realized the nature of reality and am awakened; what use have I for a wife? She would be a dream of delusion. Ps_1.20: "I have attained the state of a Buddha and am the refuge of the world; what use have I for a wife? She would be a burden of worldly duty. Ps_1.21: "I have transcended birth and death and am liberated from time; what use have I for a wife? She would be a vessel of old age and decay. Ps_1.22: "I have attained the power of the Victors and am sovereign over all; what use have I for a wife? She would be a slave to another's will. Ps_1.23: "I have realized the ultimate truth and am the light of the world; what use have I for a wife? She would be a veil of darkness. Ps_1.24: "I have attained the state of a protector and am the guide of beings; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of attachment. Ps_1.25: "I have realized the nature of the self and am without ego; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of pride. Ps_1.26: "I have attained the state of a hero and am invincible in battle; what use have I for a wife? She would be a cowardice of the heart. Ps_1.27: "I have realized the nature of phenomena and am free from conceptualization; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of discursive thought. Ps_1.28: "I have attained the state of a physician and am the healer of the world; what use have I for a wife? She would be a disease of the mind. Ps_1.29: "I have realized the nature of emptiness and am without grasping; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of clinging. Ps_1.30: "I have attained the state of a king and am the lord of dharma; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of worldly sovereignty. Ps_1.31: "I have realized the nature of dependent origination and am free from causality; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of bondage. Ps_1.32: "I have attained the state of a sage and am the teacher of gods and men; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of distraction. Ps_1.33: "I have realized the nature of the three times and am beyond time; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of temporal attachment. Ps_1.34: "I have attained the state of a conqueror and am the victor over Māra; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of defeat. Ps_1.35: "I have realized the nature of the four truths and am the knower of the path; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of deviation. Ps_1.36: "I have attained the state of a leader and am the guide to liberation; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of entanglement. Ps_1.37: "I have realized the nature of the six perfections and am the fulfiller of the path; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of obstruction. Ps_1.38: "I have attained the state of a bodhisattva and am the friend of all beings; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of enmity. Ps_1.39: "I have realized the nature of the ten powers and am the possessor of strength; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of weakness. Ps_1.40: "I have attained the state of a tathāgata and am the one who has gone thus; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of regression. Ps_1.41: "I have realized the nature of the eighteen unique qualities and am the peerless one; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of rivalry. Ps_1.42: "I have attained the state of a buddha and am the light of the universe; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of obscuration. Ps_1.43: "I have realized the nature of the thirty-two marks and am the possessor of beauty; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of ugliness. Ps_1.44: "I have attained the state of a mahāsattva and am the great being; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of smallness. Ps_1.45: "I have realized the nature of the eighty minor marks and am the possessor of grace; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of coarseness. Ps_1.46: "I have attained the state of a jina and am the conqueror of all; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of defeat. Ps_1.47: "I have realized the nature of the four fearlessnesses and am the fearless one; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of fear. Ps_1.48: "I have attained the state of a śāstṛ and am the teacher of the world; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of ignorance. Ps_1.49: "I have realized the nature of the four analytical knowledges and am the possessor of wisdom; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of delusion. Ps_1.50: "I have attained the state of a muni and am the silent sage; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of noise. Ps_1.51: "I have realized the nature of the three gates of liberation and am the gatekeeper of freedom; what use have I for a wife? She would be a source of confinement. Since this body was surrendered by me for the sake of the world, and even the Dharma is characterized by its relinquishment,
then my mind’s attachment to external objects is as inappropriate as an elephant’s ceremonial bathing.
Let those seeking meat take this flesh; let one who seeks marrow take it as well from its extraction.
For I bear this little body for the sake of the world—how much more so, then, external things?
Just as people take the bark, leaves, flowers, and so forth of a medicinal tree, yet such conceptual constructions as "these are taking what belongs to me" do not arise at all; so it is here.

In the same way, as I strive for the welfare of the world, I must not entertain even the slightest hesitation regarding this body, which is suffering, ungrateful, perpetually impure, and yet being employed for the sake of another.
Since the internal elements such as earth and water are equal to the external collection of great elements,
why is there this practice of the mud-stain of ignorance— the thought "this is mine" and "this is not mine"— even by me?
Take even my limbs as you wish; do not entertain the notion that this [body] belongs to another.
This is yours alone; why then should I have any sense of self-identification with it?

Those Buddhas, the inconceivable Great Beings, declare that excellence of a Bodhisattva— that great being— to be such when wonderful reflections conducive to the state of perfect enlightenment arise within him constantly.
Thus, that hero in the practice of generosity never develops regard even for his own body;
his actions consisting of speech, body, and mind effortlessly attain purity.
Having purified his actions, he brings about the welfare of others without the suffering of exertion;
thus, through his earnest striving for the sake of sentient beings, he attains skill in discerning what is right and what is wrong.
Having obtained even greater power through that gift, he then effects, by means of the gift of the true Dharma,
a clearer illumination for people wandering in the darkness of existence, like the light from the rising of the sun.
The accomplishment of the welfare of the world is common [to all], as is the establishment in the exalted state of omniscience;
therefore, his merit arises inexhaustibly, like the radiance of the sun established in its rising.
Thus, these marvelous floods of qualities consisting of giving become the ornaments of a bodhisattva;
therefore, the mind should be prepared for that giving which is preceded by compassion.
By means of this, may I bring about for the worlds the Buddha-qualities such as longevity, eloquence, and power;
and may sentient beings, gathered by me through material gifts, also become vessels for the True Dharma.
Thus the wise one, moving for the sake of the world, bestows the gift of food not for the sake of attaining the splendors of heaven,
but also gives drinks to quench the thirst of the afflictions of the world.

Thinking, "How might the entire world become a recipient of the Buddha’s miraculous powers, his various activities, and the bliss of nirvāṇa? the Lord of the World bestows the Great Vehicle, for he delights in the Mahāyāna.
And for the sake of accomplishing the praise of the Perfectly Awakened One, which possesses the luster of gold, as well as the ornament consisting of modesty itself,
he respectfully provides noble garments at the appropriate times.
Beholding the seat of the terrace of enlightenment, the thrones, and the three couches,
he offered garlands of lamps at the shrines and along the streets in order to obtain the eye of omniscience.

One who is intent upon becoming a refuge gives musical instruments for the sake of gathering divine sounds, and offers incense as a gift to those of awakened virtue; one also gives assembly halls, water-stations, gardens, monasteries, and dwellings.
The gift of well-prepared flavors is given for the sake of attaining the excellence of both the finest and the least refined tastes;
the gifts of medicine are given to lead these worlds to freedom from old age and death.
Desiring to lead those worlds who had been reduced to slavery by a multitude of afflictions to a state of freedom equal to his own,
he constantly gave away male and female slaves and others, never turning away those who were already servants or even lower than servants.

Because he loves awakening, he gives blameless gifts, bestowing sons, daughters, and beloved ones; and because he delights in the singular joy of the true Dharma, he grants excellent diversions that serve as causes for delight.
He gives gold, pearls, gems, coral, and so forth for the sake of the perfection of the primary marks;
and he gives various ornaments radiant with jewels for the excellence of the secondary characteristics.

For the sake of meditation, he tirelessly gives away gardens and groves of asceticism; for the treasury of the True Dharma, he gives away his treasury of wealth; and for the sovereignty of the King of Sages, he gives away kingdoms adorned with the power of command.
With his two supreme feet marked by wheels, out of eagerness to tread upon the seat of enlightenment,
he— remaining unchanging— bestows the gift of his feet, which accomplishes the welfare of the world.
"How could I not extend my hands to the world submerged in the river of suffering that flows so very swiftly?
Thus he offers his hands, which shine like blossoming lotuses, as the hands of the True Dharma.
In order to fulfill the faculty of faith and the others, he gives away his ears, nose, and so forth without weariness;
and he gives his eyes, desiring to purify the vision of the world by abandoning all obscurations.

The Protector cuts off his flesh along with its blood and gives it away out of compassion; how might this body of mine become like earth, fire, wind, and water, so that it may be a source of sustenance for the world?
For the sake of attaining the supramundane supreme knowledge, he honors [his teachers] even with his head;
how much more so, then, does he honor supplicants who have approached him with other parts of his body?
How could I, whose heroic deeds are so wondrous, not give even my marrow to the world? For I am the body of the Tathāgata, invincible even by a rain of falling, blazing thunderbolts.
Thus, this constant and blameless rain of the water of generosity, released by the cloud that is the bodhisattva,
having gladdened the entire world, flows into the ocean of omniscience.
Having sought out enjoyments, he does not give them by dishonest means nor by oppressing another;
he does not do so for the sake of removing fear or shame, nor while searching for those worthy of offerings.

Nor, when there is something excellent, should one despise it by giving what is coarse, thinking "this is not worthy of offerings," or give with a mind made wretched by a longing for the karmic result, or give without respect, or give what is loathsome. (Ps 1.37)
Bestowing honor upon one who possesses virtue, he does not fall into the opposite state toward another;
he neither exalts himself nor disparages another, for his application is impartial.
He has no gift with a false intention, nor does he have any gift lacking resolute intent;
he gives nothing impaired by the fault of anger, nor does he feel regret after having given.

He does not give a great gift when being praised, nor does he give something else when not being praised; he gives no gift that causes harm to beggars, nor anything that might become a cause for their misconduct.
He gives nothing at an improper time; he gives only at the right time, even in difficult circumstances.
He does not give for the sake of becoming a god, nor for the sake of sovereignty, nor out of a longing for the inferior vehicle.

He does not give with a view toward looking at his own face, nor for the sake of fame or reputation, nor for the sake of laughter; nor does he think, "This is enough for me," nor does he laugh at others out of malice. (Ps 1.42)
He never gives a gift that is not dedicated toward the state of omniscience or one that is censurable;
therefore, his giving attains supreme purity, which is designated as a perfection (pāramitā).

Even if all the merit arising from his giving were gathered together from the entire world, it could never surpass that mass of merit; for that reason, he attains the state of being the Supreme Being in the world.

For one whose self is firmly established in the five superknowledges, as for the rain of gifts that he pours down upon the world, how could there be any measure or exhaustion, since it flows forth continuously? (Ps 1.45)
That which is the cause of inexhaustible wisdom for the benefit of inexhaustible worlds is not defiled by the perishable threefold world, just as the sky is not defiled by clouds.
It is concentrated on the aspect of emptiness and is entirely free from the defects of signs;
because it is established as the dissociation from the afflictions of "nothingness," it is declared by the Lords of Sages to be inexhaustible.
Furthermore, in this *Satpuruṣāvadāna*, which is the cause of the expansion of happiness through generosity,
one who desires to practice yoga should cultivate the perception of impermanence regarding enjoyments and compassion for the world.
Perceiving enjoyments as impermanent, and once compassion has become his very nature, he reaches the firm conviction: "That which is given away is truly mine; that which remains in my house is not."

That which is given brings no fear to us at any time in the home, whereas from that [which is kept] fear approaches; what is shared must be guarded and fails to satisfy, but when it is given, these misfortunes have no power over one.
That which is given brings happiness even in the next world, while that which is not given produces suffering right here;
for wealth has the nature of a torch, and if not relinquished, it brings calamity to men.
That which is not given goes to destruction; indeed, that which is given attains the state of a treasure.
For that which is bestowed by one intent on the welfare of the world is the true essence of wealth, which is otherwise pithless and trivial.
That which is given by the wise is praiseworthy, and even a foolish person praises such accumulation;
for generally, there is separation from possessions, yet from giving arises prosperity and fame.
That which is given does not lead to the grasping of afflictions, nor does it lead to affliction; stinginess is an ignoble quality.
That which is given is the true path; therefore, the Noble Ones declare that what is otherwise is the wrong path.
When a supplicant arrives as a cause for increasing the equipment for enlightenment,
one should regard oneself as his servant and cultivate affection for that spiritual friend toward him.
Since the passions and other afflictions of great-souled ones diminish upon hearing a petitioner,
their arrival at the door of a petitioner is dearer to them than even the coming of a festival.
If, moreover, even when a beggar has arrived, he is unable to give because of extreme weakness,
he should conciliate that beggar with sweet and gentle words so that he does not become angry.
And he should exert effort for the sake of restraining stinginess and abandoning delusion,
in such a way that the beggar never turns away from him dejected or discouraged.

How could one who harbors even a trace of stinginess toward material goods ever possess the mind of awakening? For a person of pure mind is not defiled by faults, just as the ocean is not defiled by corpses.
Therefore, having abandoned all faults in every respect, one who seeks awakening should always be a giver of everything;
where is this mind of a lone hero intent on saving the worlds, and where is this wretched, lackluster exertion? (Ps 1.60)
The root of this gift is the mind of perfect awakening; one who wishes to give such a gift must not abandon it.
The Perfect Buddhas declare that person to be the foremost among givers who desires to practice supreme renunciation within the worlds.
