2. A Summary of the Perfection of Ethical Discipline (Śīlapāramitā):

In order to make people delightful by adorning them with the ethical discipline of a Perfectly Awakened One, one should first purify one's own ethical discipline with arisen earnestness; for ethical discipline bestows the power of capability.
One should establish such love for the world that even in a dream one has no taste for malice;
having the sole essence of benefiting others, one should not touch the enjoyments of others, as if they were snakes.
One whose mind has turned away from the engagement in dualities, even before forming an attachment to a spouse,
should perform with his body the deeds of a virtuous person, acting for the sake of the welfare of the world.

Having desisted from that which is contrary to it, one should speak words that are sweet and pleasing, appropriate for the occasion, truthful, conducive to the goal, and non-divisive, for the sake of attaining the reality of the true Dharma.
Whatever task was to be performed by me with effort has been accomplished by him through his own means;
thus, with a mind full of joy regarding the happiness of another, one should cultivate a state of mind free from covetousness toward objects of the heart.

This is my own weakness, that this person, being powerless under the influence of afflictions, does not know his own welfare; even regarding the transgressions of others, one must thus exert effort to extinguish the fire of malice.
Having dispelled the expansion of darkness consisting of false views from the mind by means of the light of knowledge,
one should cultivate an unshakeable devotion toward the Best of Men and Gods, its roots grown deep through the practice of his virtues.
One should never deviate from these paths of action, which are the true paths to heaven and liberation;
for those who abide here, their specific thoughts for the welfare of the world become fruitful.
In brief, they say that this morality is the restraint of body, speech, and mind;
since it is entirely contained within these very [three], one should therefore purify them without effort.
One whose inclination is toward abstaining from violence bestows well-being upon people by virtue of his gentle nature;
furthermore, he effortlessly eradicates whatever latent tendencies for faults exist in his mind. (Ps 2.10)
When the mind is permeated by a special state of loving-kindness and the persistence of enmity has been stilled,
one awakens in happiness and sleeps in happiness, free from the defects of evil dreams and mental disturbances.
Even the *rakṣas* spirits provide him protection, and he encounters no fear of miserable rebirths;
he attains a long life, delightful with the quality of health, and firmly established in a happy destiny.

And therefore, for the Tathāgatas who have attained perfect enlightenment, there arises a wind that follows the power of their minds, performing immeasurable labor for the sake of increasing the happiness of the world.
But he who does not take the enjoyments of another obtains great enjoyments in the next world—
enjoyments that cannot be seized by hosts of kingly heirs, just as mountains cannot be shaken by the wind.
Through purity of conduct, one attains here and now the state of being beloved and becoming a vessel of trust;
therefore, free from hesitation in undertaking the welfare of others, one never encounters an obstruction to one's progress.
One who possesses pure ethical discipline effortlessly develops the realization that the expansion of wealth is without essence;
therefore, with a mind purified of secondary afflictions, one personally attains unsurpassed awakening.
Having desisted from misconduct regarding sensual pleasures due to his mastery over the senses, and finding delight in tranquility,
he attains fame on all sides through the world’s praises, spreading to the very ends of the quarters.
Nor does he harbor any passion for women, regarding them as if they were his own mothers;
and from this accumulation of merit, the Lord of Sages is born with the secret store of an elephant.

Turning away from false speech, full of joy and with a mind free from deceit, he effortlessly causes sentient beings to turn toward the Dharma through the authoritative success of his words. (Ps 2.19)
That he who loves truth becomes dear even to the dwellers of heaven is not so wonderful;
for it is the very nature of the gods to favor virtue, and they were eyewitnesses to his deeds.
That he has become an authority and is beloved by worldly people—this is what is marvelous here;
for generally the world is poor in virtues and judges others according to its own [limited] inference. (Ps_2.21)
As if having abandoned groves of blue lotuses, the delightful and pleasing fragrance, seeking out excellence, takes refuge in her face which acts like a white lotus.
Beholding with radiant wisdom that delivers one from miserable rebirths— wisdom that distinguishes between the equal and the unequal—
that person, being a witness to their own self, feels shame even for accidental unwholesome thoughts.
Thus, being of pure nature, he is gradually neither suspected by others nor does he suspect others;
consequently, his speech, which conforms to truth, attains inviolability in the state of a Tathāgata.
The body is invulnerable to the attacks of others; his excellence of retinue is such that it cannot be led astray by others;
for one who has abandoned slander, his faith becomes indivisible, having the practice of the Dharma as its essence.
He attains an unbreakable and unfailing loving-kindness, and never abandons compassion for the sake of the world;
furthermore, he gains a most unbreakable assembly of disciples even in other births while abiding in the state of a sage.
The spreading dust at the vanguard of the army of anger, scattered by the fierce winds of volition,
which destroys the body of one’s reputation— this harsh speech should be cast aside by the clouds of loving-kindness.
Having desisted from this [harmful conduct], he wins over the hearts of the world with sweet words;
and when affection for him has taken root in the world, those very same words of his become even more acceptable.

Therefore, having disciplined hundreds of worlds and having closed off for them the path of suffering, the one of meritorious karma does not go to an evil rebirth; for Dharma indeed protects both in this world and in the next.
Even from afar, its clear resonance of syllables is heard; though nearby, it is of a pleasant nature. More majestic than the roar of a cloud, this Brahma-voice of his adorns his face.
One who refrains from incoherent speech attains absolute favor among the wise;
through truthful expression, one's intellect advances and one attains genuine greatness.

And because of these merits, when he is questioned regarding the profound and hidden matters within the state of a King of Sages, he explains even many questions at a single time with his speech, free from doubt. (Ps 2.32)
Having abandoned with his intellect covetousness— which is never barren of harmful fruits both in this world and after death—
he attains, through a state free from envy, a far more extensive prosperity that he deeply desires.
When the mind is purified, the actions of speech and body that depend upon it become pure,
like the circles of stars in the expanse of the sky, which is beautiful with the quality of darkness.
Through the sovereign power of merit, his intellect always inclines toward the most excellent enjoyments;
he attains the esteem of kings as well as invincibility against those who are arrogant.
His faculties do not undergo deficiency, for they possess the power produced by virtuous deeds;
and thus he alone becomes a Teacher worthy of worship in the three worlds, possessing an irreversible wheel.
Freed from the fever of malice and burning passion, he manifests a noble disposition through his conduct;
indeed, by his healthy and tranquil movements, he makes manifest the clarity of his mind.
Even when faced with actions that are violent in nature, associated with conflict, unworthy of noble ones, or deceitful,
his mind never turns toward them, because he has attained the distinguished experience of the bliss of loving-kindness.
In this world, he attains equality with the noble ones and is honored by people like a deity;
even the world of Brahmā is not difficult to reach for him whose path of mind is smooth and pliable through his deeds.
Delighting in the welfare of the world, he effortlessly gladdens the minds of beings,
just as the lovely autumn season clarifies the waters of rivers that were turbid from the arrival of the clouds.
By means of his form, which is beloved by all to behold, his basis for knowledge, and his wondrous conduct,
he seems to unify the world’s perception of distinctness regarding consciousness within the state of sagehood.
Shining while treading through the mire of false views, he attains companions with virtuous hearts;
and realizing "I am the owner of my actions," he does not commit even a sinful deed, even when being executed.
His devotion to the Victor becomes unshakable, and he is no longer led astray by superstitious omens and auspicious charms;
he gains a firm footing on the noble path and thereby attains the state of progressing toward excellence.
Having emerged from the view of a self-identity, he does not go to an evil rebirth because the causes have been exhausted;
endowed with unobstructed knowledge, he wanders through heaven and earth without attachment.
Furthermore, even those qualities not yet attained by the Pratyekabuddhas all become manifest to him;
for the dharmas of the Lord of Sages, expanding for the sake of the welfare of the world, lead to the state of omniscience.

What wise person indeed would not embrace this manifestation, variegated with the jewels of virtue, praiseworthy, and delightful through its qualities that are spontaneously grasped—especially one who desires the welfare of sentient beings? (Ps 2.46)

If there were virtue (śīla), what wonder would there be in this—that among humans there is a divine and delightful prosperity, whose sole flavor is supreme happiness, and from which even the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma) sprout forth? (Ps 2.47)
But one who has fallen from morality is incapable even of his own welfare; how then could he be capable of accomplishing the welfare of others?
Therefore, for one who strives specifically for the sake of others, it is not right to be lax in one's regard for this [morality]. (Ps 2.48)
Observing the intense danger therein, one should avoid even the slightest thing that ought to be avoided;
nor should one, for the sake of one's own pleasure, violate the ethical discipline (śīla) appropriate for a bodhisattva.

One should not allow one's virtue to become mottled by the defects of broken precepts, nor by being worn down by the pleasures of women, massages, and sights, nor by the afflictions and attachments of wicked people. (Ps 2.50)
One should practice a morality that is free from the stain of blemish through the accumulation of absolute purity;
it is independent in its course like the conduct of a freed slave, and is irreproachable, adorned with the praise of the wise.
And through the fulfillment of all the precepts, it is complete and free from resentment;
by means of intense practices that have the sole flavor of the welfare of others and which are like reflections of the purity of mind.
Through the restraint of the senses based on mindfulness, one should be intent on the preservation of ethical conduct,
like the thousand-rayed sun dispelling the darkness of the world's prevailing immorality.

With a mind fully contented by means obtained through righteous means— such as the application of ointments and bandaging for bodily wounds, which are employed merely as remedies against suffering— one should be wary of looking toward others with envy.
Even while abiding in all things worthy of praise— those conducive to virtuous conduct and the arising of good qualities—
one should not be conceited because of being free from pride, and one should fear for one’s reputation arising therefrom.
For gain, by revealing one's virtues, turns into enmity through the mouth of a friend;
just as the cool-rayed moon destroys the welfare of lotuses, it ruins those whose vows are lax.
They say that ethical discipline is the method for cultivating virtues, and all virtues are contained within the mind of awakening;
since that [mind] is cultivated through the virtue of compassion, one should therefore always possess the discipline of compassion. (Ps 2.57)
That which, being independent, does not abide even in the realm of desire, nor in the realm of form,
and which does not abide in the formless realm— that, they declare, is virtue in its true sense.

One who, for the sake of the welfare of the world, practices ethical discipline in order to establish all beings throughout immeasurable world-systems in that same discipline—that is called a "perfection" (pāramitā) by those who know it. (Ps_2.59)
Ethical discipline is the path to the attainment of excellence, the inheritance of those whose nature is compassion;
it is the pure essence of the preeminence of knowledge, a supreme form of adornment that eliminates all arrogance.
An ointment with a pleasing fragrance that pervades the three worlds is not incompatible with the life of one who has gone forth;
yet it distinguishes men from ordinary people of similar appearance by means of their moral conduct. (Ps 2.61)
Because of his steadfastness even without boasting, and without the exertion of verbal disputes,
he possesses a lordship that has abandoned the arrogance of pride, by which all the world is bowed down without being commanded.

Even for those men who are unacquainted and unknown, who do not engage in social intimacy or praise, and who perform no essential service, yet remain steadfast in the pure practice of moral discipline; [even for them, the Dharma is beneficial].

Mortals and gods bear upon their crest-tips the dust that has been purified by resting on the feet [of the noble] and obtained through prostration; therefore, virtue is more glorious than noble birth. (Ps 2.64)

Therefore, one should not practice stainless morality out of fear of miserable rebirths, nor for the sake of sovereignty, nor from the arising of a desire for the riches of heaven; for it would not be so [if practiced thus]. Rather, one should cultivate morality as the supreme means for accomplishing the welfare of the world.
// A Summary of the Perfection of Ethical Discipline //
They say that the illusion of the side of the god of love is delusive, yet they call the illusion of liberation blissful;
why then would one not exert effort toward that patience which is exclusively beneficial? // Ps_3.1 //
The steadfast composure of the virtuous, which is always unacquainted with offenses against others, is pleasing to the mind;
it is a beautiful perception produced by their virtues—patience, which acts for the sake of the world through the wisdom of compassion. (Ps 3.2)
For those whose minds are intent upon the welfare of others, they say that endurance is the foremost initiation;
for like a dam across waters, it holds back the faults of anger and obstructs the higher goods of the world.
For those endowed with power, the wealth of asceticism is adorned by the excellence of strength;
patience is a stream of water for the forest fire of malice, bringing the cessation of misfortune both in this world and after death.
Upon the armor of patience worn by the virtuous, the arrows of the wicked's words are blunted;
for the most part, they turn into flowers of praise and become components of the garland of their fame.
The counteraction to the poison of the wicked’s speech is the radiance of the moon of knowledge;
the natural disposition of the steadfast ascetics is patience, the dwelling place of all virtues. (Ps 3.6)
The essence of the profound being is the arrival of thick clouds to quench the heat of the affliction of anger;
when the time has passed, the pervasive sound consisting of patience arises from that ocean of virtues.
This series of steps, free from the defect of weariness, leads upward as far as the Brahma-world;
it is a workshop for the final completion of his form, which is adorned with the excellence of the primary marks and the secondary signs.
Patience is the river that uproots the great trees of faults laden with the fruit of enmity;
it is ever-favorable to the ocean of the qualities of the fully developed spirit of enlightenment.
Wholesomeness brings prosperity and benefit even in the next world; it is the supreme increase for one whose purpose is the welfare of the world.
Patience is the accomplishment of an excellence of wholesome nature and the purification of mind, body, and speech.
Not cut off by the defects of saṃsāra, as he gazes upon sentient beings with the tenderness of compassion,
he seems to attain a state consisting entirely of glory throughout the world through his virtuous deeds that benefit the world.
He is not touched by the faults of words expressing wonder, for he is patient through the purity of his knowledge;
and because of the arising of the power of patience regarding impermanence, he does not experience even the slightest elation when encountering pleasure.
He does not shrink from ill repute because he relies on the power of patience;
and for this reason, because he is independent of all other worldly conditions, he is not fickle.
Even by means of violent injuries, the minds of the virtuous do not undergo transformation;
for they possess a firm aspiration toward the state of a Lord of Sages and are well-prepared through the empowerment of patience.
With a mind steadfast in patience, he undertakes arduous austerities solely out of a desire for their welfare,
intending to humble the pride and arrogance in the hearts of the heretics.

This world, deluded by its attachment to a self and conceiving others as "the rest," has its mind overcome by various forms of that [self-attachment]; through the lack of patience, it falls into exhaustion. (Ps 3.16)
The minds of the virtuous, supported by compassion and having performed the rite of protection through patience,
do not undergo transformation due to injuries from others, because they have abandoned the view of a self and out of their affection for virtue.
False conceptualization is the cause of the fever of the heart and of anger for those weak in fortitude;
but right conceptualization brings about the various forms of peace in the mind through patience.
When one relies upon patience that is based on conceptual construction, there will be no opportunity for wavering;
it is like the disappearance of the reflection of the full moon in water rippled by the morning breeze.
Those who know the reality of forbearance say that, in the ultimate sense, forbearance is the pacification of conceptual construction;
therefore, observing the world as like a dream, one should strive for the cessation of conceptual construction.
Does the eye revile? This eye, or the ear and so forth—does that revile? Such forbearance is merely an investigation into the sense-bases; it is not patience in the ultimate sense.

The speaker and this speech are indeed impermanent; even this conceptualization of mine is a construction of impermanent phenomena. They do not call this [state] the supreme patient acceptance. (Ps 3.22)
There is no one who performs an injury, nor is there anyone by whom an action is performed;
this is the accomplishment of the vision of selflessness, and it is patience that has reached its ultimate limit.
Dependent upon this or that, there arise various states: notions of blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
Since these are established through dependence, they are a ground for entry; yet this patience is utterly composed.

If, when one's mind is overturned by the great seizure of delusion, one thinks, "I am certainly not like this," then what opportunity is there for the excellence of patience when the mind is both elated and dejected? (Ps 3.25)
Perishing as it is uttered one by one like an echo from a machine of fragmented syllables—how, to whom, and what kind of suffering could even this most excellent patience cause? (3.26)
If she does not regard even her own suffering for the sake of exhausting my sins, then she is indeed a most excellent friend to us; for she acts solely through the practice of forbearance.
For it is by observing the very sovereignty of karma and by seeing its qualities that one endures;
for even such a form of patience, when afflicted by conceptual construction, does not lead to the state of steadfastness.
I tolerate impermanence, suffering, impurity, and the lack of intrinsic nature, but not their opposites;
this is a tolerance capable of pacifying opposing factors through the engagement with duality, but it is not ultimate.
A person who is discerning regarding the reality of things effortlessly engages in acts of benefiting others;
yet patience does not attain such equanimity, for patience is not thus [effortless] as long as conceptual construction has not been exhausted.
When the successive stages of conceptualization, which are inferior to meditative absorption, come to an end without remainder,
those who travel the path of non-duality speak of that as the unsurpassed patience, the domain of the equanimous.
Just as no entities whatsoever arise from themselves, from another, from both, or without a cause;
so too, no entities whatsoever cease from themselves, from another, from both, or without a cause.

An effect is never found anywhere—whether from what is destroyed, from what is not destroyed, from both, or from neither; nevertheless, an effect arises from a real entity. Such is the capacity that is devoid of duality; it is the capacity. (Ps 3.33)
There is no birth of either the existent or the non-existent; without birth, there is no cessation for anything anywhere.
For one who perceives that all things are empty of intrinsic nature, the ultimate patient acceptance arises.
Having attained this [prediction], he will be proclaimed by thousands of Victors as "He shall become a Victor";
and for him who is ever concentrated, the practice of acting for the welfare of the world proceeds.
As long as the intellect remains attached to the existence of things, for that long one encounters duality here through delusion;
likewise, the signless, which is the cause of liberation, remains as far from him as the sky is from the earth.
He attains mastery over the deeds of dedication to the Dharma, over supernatural powers, resolute faith, and rebirth;
likewise over the arrangement of requisites within his own mind, over preeminent wisdom, and over the lifespan.
Having obtained this supreme wealth consisting of mastery— which is imperishable and the means for accomplishing the welfare of others—
he becomes a powerful support for people who are falling into hardships.

Therefore, those who bear the great burden of the welfare of others should always follow this method of patience. For one established in this, all actions— adorned with the fruits of virtue— become delightful through the intention to benefit others.
For even devotion that has taken deep root in this [teaching] is practiced by sages for the sake of attaining the state of a king among sages;
indeed, for those whose minds are permeated by faith, no breakage of the axle of the chariot of their desires is ever seen on the path of Dharma.
// A Summary of the Perfection of Patience //
4. A Summary of the Perfection of Vigor:
Once he has become established in the power of patience that endures all things, he undertakes all wonders through his heroism;
for by means of vigor, which possesses the great strength that brings tasks to completion, he surpasses even the gods. (Ps_4.1)
Even worldly tasks, though their further limits are clearly visible, become difficult to cross when one lacks vigor;
yet there is nothing whose form is unattainable for one whose prowess is free from weariness.
The inferior one exerts effort only at the start, while the mediocre one falls into despondency after having begun;
those whose valor is untiring for the sake of others undertake their task, setting aside even their own nirvāṇa.
Generally, this person, though possessing self-dependent strength, has his own tasks made heavy by being overcome with dejection;
but for one whose vigor is undiminished, even a burden of others' work as solid as Mount Meru can be accomplished without weariness.

If the days at both ends of the cycle of existence were equal in their effortlessness and worthlessness, and if those years, accumulated over exceedingly long kalpas, were like drops of water in the ocean; // Ps_4.5 //
If I were to generate the thought of awakening with this same effort one by one,
I would still accumulate the remainder of the provisions, having further cast off weariness and dejection.
Even if each single thought of awakening were to be attained in this manner, along with the remaining methods for accumulating the provisions,
I would still bring enlightenment to full realization, possessing the strength of fortitude impelled by compassion.
Without reflecting on the suffering of cyclic existence, they maintain an inconceivable firmness of armor;
this, they say, is the primary undertaking of those whose nature is compassion and who observe the vow of heroes.
Having traversed on foot the entire earth, which is like glowing embers and strewn with weapons,
he is able even to behold the Lords of Sages or to drink the auspicious elixir of the Dharma.

"Having lifted these people out of the mire of saṃsāra, I shall establish them in the bliss of nirvāṇa"—thus does the mind itself apply itself to the process of lifting up and setting down the steps. (Ps 4.10)
Or, when one’s mind proceeds toward the welfare of another, or toward merits for the benefit of the world—
that is the second form of valorous exertion among those of inexhaustible prowess, in the practice of assuming glorious qualities.

And that which is the dedication toward the state of perfect buddhahood at the very moment merit arises—that virtuous undertaking they declare to be for the sake of attaining inexhaustibility. (Ps 4.12)
Just as a drop of water poured into great bodies of water never undergoes exhaustion,
even so there is no depletion of merit that has been dedicated toward the state of perfect enlightenment.

For it is thus: "These merits bear fruit for the sake of the state of omniscience for the world of the moving and the unmoving"; with a mind purified by compassion, that noble being undertakes them accordingly.
No one could extinguish the flood of beings throughout the great trichiliocosm in a single day;
likewise, even in an eon, not even a single being of the realm of sentient beings would be brought to maturity by him.

Having heard of this inexhaustibility of beings, for one who truly desires to lead all beings without exception and whose vigor is not swallowed by the fault of despondency— what essential goal here remains far out of reach for such a person?
The entire mass of merit belonging to all worlds, multiplied tenfold by that same measure, results in a single pore of the Conqueror’s skin;
and each such pore possesses a single, well-formed hair.
By that merit, which is increased a hundredfold and resides in each pore of his skin, a single secondary mark (anuvyañjana) is produced; by the remainder of it, all the others arise upon his body.
And from that very mass of merit, consisting of those same qualities,
there arises for him the variegated work of the primary marks, each one individually proclaiming his state of a Jina, which is entered into by the secondary characteristics.

From merit multiplied a thousandfold, which serves as the cause for the arising of the primary marks, there is produced for him the *ūrṇā*, beautiful in color and possessing a radiance as clear as the full moon. (Ps 4.20)
And the karma that produces the *ūrṇā* (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows) is merit multiplied by hundreds of thousands;
it creates for him a head adorned with a *uṣṇīṣa*, which resembles a royal parasol and is impossible to look upon directly.

Thinking, "I must accumulate this treasury of merit for the sake of others," when one is oriented toward vigor within the supreme bodhicitta, by what means could an inclination toward indolence find entry therein? (Ps 4.22)
Even if all sentient beings in the world-system were equal to Pratyekabuddhas, a single Bodhisattva established in patience would indeed possess superior power in wisdom compared to them. (Ps 4.23)

In the same way, one who possesses tireless vigor in the application of wholesome qualities—both mundane and supramundane—attains a distinction over those established in the power of patience, such that they become irreversible. (Ps 4.24)
Even further removed from them is one who is bound to enlightenment by only one more birth;
what need is there to speak of those possessed of firm vigor who have already sat down for the first time at the foot of the Bodhi tree?
Even if the entire world-system were filled to the brim with such purity of knowledge,
it would not equal even a fraction of the power of one standing at the foot of the Bodhi tree who has brought about the final destruction of the enemy Māra.
If all worlds without exception were to possess minds purified by such knowledge, they would still not equal even a fraction, however minute, of the Sage’s power. (Ps 4.27)
Thus, alone, he whose nature is compassion sets out to cross the ocean of wondrous gnosis;
his command is unimpeded in the movements of others' minds, and his light of wisdom pervades the vast expanse of space.
Toward all sentient beings, there arises in him a mother-like affection and compassion that is equal;
and from that, all the remaining marvelous qualities of a perfectly awakened Buddha arise without exception.
Endowed with these qualities of undertaking, which are like pure ears for those of feeble strength,
he shines forth even more through the excellence of his vigor, like the path of reality with its eight branches.
Vigor is threefold: it is the application to what is wholesome, and from that, the excellence of speech, body, and mind;
it belongs to one who has set out, who is established, and who is concentrated, being the preeminent vigor consisting of the mind.
That which is the cultivation of the thought of awakening, equanimity, compassion, and patience regarding selflessness;
the gathering of people through the four means of attraction, and non-attachment toward all phenomena. (Ps 4.32)

That there is no weariness in the mire of saṃsāra, and that the triple world itself is not perceived; that there is the gift of all one's possessions, yet no pride because of it; and that there is no pride regarding the complete training, nor on account of the training itself. (Ps 4.33)
Fortitude that remains unshaken by injuries from others, and the absolute undisturbedness of the mind;
steadfastness in undertakings for wholesome deeds, and a joy in the mind whose sole flavor is seclusion.

Entering the fourfold meditative absorptions and the mental realization of selflessness; insatiability regarding the breadth of learning, and entry into the method through the investigation thereof. (Ps 4.35)

The teaching itself, the knowledge of things as they have been heard, the ineffability of phenomena, mastery over the five superknowledges, and the mere cultivation for that which is beyond—these constitute [the path]. (Ps 4.36)
That which is the accomplishment of the bases of psychic power, an activity that is both skillful and free from exertion;
and that which is the application in the right efforts, and the liberation precisely from the wholesome and unwholesome. // Ps_4.37 //
Whatever skill he has in determining the faculties, he perceives both the faculty-less and all phenomena;
he seeks the equipment for the path and its investigation, yet there is no going anywhere for him from anywhere at all.
Such is this [practice], possessing vast and diverse heroic vigor, variegated by its distinctions of setting forth and remaining established.
For the sake of fulfilling its inexhaustibility, the very act of setting forth is the specific cause.
He does not engage even in actions motivated by signs, yet he abides in action consisting of wisdom;
due to the quality of compassion, he does not abandon the conditioned, and though possessing great vigor, he does not fall into the unconditioned.

The hearing of unprecedented Dharma, freedom from minor ailments, invincibility, the retention of the heard Dharma, the acquisition of protection even from non-human beings, and the attainment of the lineage of meditative concentration; // Ps_4.41 //

For day and night his actions proceed without fail; nor does he suffer any decline in his qualities, which—like a lotus, ever increasing—are superior to the nature of ordinary men and serve a far greater purpose.

Wide renown, happiness that brings forth further happiness, a supreme mind free from wretchedness, and those qualities pertaining to this very life—all these arise from vigor; what wonder is there in this? (Ps 4.43)

When even those who possess immeasurable virtues and are worthy of worship by the three worlds attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha by relying on the firm application of vigor, then who could possibly not be devoted to vigor? (4.44)
// A Summary of the Perfection of Vigor //
5. Summary of the Perfection of Meditation (Dhyānapāramitā).

Now, one should apply oneself to the practice of meditation for the increase of knowledge, so that by means of the light of knowledge, one may easily bring about the welfare and grace of the world. (Ps_5.1)
Knowledge becomes exceedingly clear within the mind made pure by meditation,
just as the orb of the moon shines in the sky when the clouds have been driven away by autumn.
Possessing pure ethical discipline, accompanied by virtuous, beneficial companions,
having few worldly duties, with a tranquil self, and enveloped in the foundation of mindfulness.
Dwelling at the roots of trees on ground covered with green grass,
in places naturally beautiful and unadorned, fragrant with the scents of forest flowers.
In those houses of contented people, steadfast through the assistance of meditation, which remained as if in a profound state due to the silence of human clamor; Ps_5.5 //
In hermitages situated in the forest or in desolate places, and in mountain groves resounding with the roars of lions; Ps_5.6 //
In whatever place free from the afflictions of social contact, sitting comfortably in the cross-legged posture and holding the body erect; Ps_5.7 //
Having established the protection consisting of mindfulness directly within the heart,
he acted as if out of compassion issuing a proclamation against unfavorable thoughts.
This is my time for the cultivation of wisdom, not for final liberation;
for I do not venture to enter nirvana myself without having first brought sentient beings to nirvana.
Thus, one who regards the welfare of the world and has set his aspiration on the state of Buddhahood should exert himself in the undertaking of meditation through constant application.
For one who churns fire while resting repeatedly would not obtain it;
likewise, even in yoga, there is no attainment of distinction without continuous application.
One should bind the mind firmly to a single object of focus;
for grasping at various other objects only agitates and afflicts the mind.
Through clear vision and the power of vigor, one should uplift the mind as it sinks; and as it becomes agitated, one should restrain it through tranquility.
Having correctly attained equanimity and being immovable by the power of concentration,
one should remain absorbed even in that state for the sake of attaining the wisdom of the Sugata.
Nor should one fall into dependence on the relish for the pleasure of meditative absorption;
for this extensive undertaking is not for the sake of one's own pleasure alone.
One who clings to body and life, with a mind struck by dejection,
should not allow his vigor to slacken even if his own head were ablaze.
Having observed the signs that his mind is falling away from concentration, he should again apply it with attentive mindfulness. (Ps 5.17)
One should turn the mind away from the hindrances by means of their opposites,
just as one turns back a wild elephant roaming at will by pulling it with a goad.
Then, his mind restored to health by the destruction of the disease of the hindrances,
he was as if liberated from poverty and as if freed from a great calamity.
With a mind imbued with joy, one should contemplate the faults of desire and the supreme succession of happiness to be found upon its relinquishment.
Flickering as fleetingly as lightning, having the nature of foam and raiment, their taste is as fragile as a dream; they have arisen, as it were, for the sake of deception.
Among fathers for their sons, and among sons for their fathers,
as well as among friends for their friends— those who constitute the very essence of affection.
Of him who was bound by an accumulation of virtues, whose essence of steadfastness was displayed even in well-arrayed battles, and who broke through the embankment of affection; ||| 5.23 ||
Since sensual desires are the cause of the suffering of seeking them here and of hell in the next world, one should not desire them.
When discursive thought, which relies upon this [mind], causes even the eye of wisdom to close, it proceeds to the detriment of both oneself and others. (Ps 5.25)
How could one who desires the welfare of others, having abandoned those sensual pleasures that even those desiring their own self avoid in every way, ever recall them with longing? (Ps 5.26)
For them, there is no satisfaction through attainment, nor by practicing day after day, nor even by accumulation;
what other disease is greater than this?
When one, struck by the taste for them, does not even perceive their own true interest, what sensible person would remember those things which are like the drinking of a madman? (Ps 5.28)
As he thus perceives sensual desires as corrupt in every respect,
his mind contracts from them and finds serene confidence in renunciation.
From that, one attains the joy and happiness born of seclusion, arising from the acquisition of pliancy,
and the one-pointedness of mind known as the first dhyāna.
Cultivating the faultiness of applied and sustained thought just as he had previously cultivated that of sensual desires,
he, seeking their pacification, experienced the bliss born of concentration and joy.
Due to internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind,
the peerless great seers call that the second dhyāna.
Then, seeing the fluctuation of the mind and becoming dispassionate toward that joy,
he attains the third dhyāna, which is endowed with mindfulness and equanimity.
Having abandoned even the enjoyment of pleasure, and being free from both pleasure and pain,
one attains the fourth dhyāna, which is purified by mindfulness and equanimity.
And there he attains the five superknowledges that follow him,
just as a righteous king established in his realm possesses modesty, fame, glory, majesty, and splendor.
And those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, having surpassed those attained by Pratyekajinas,
become far superior through the accomplishment of the welfare of others.
For he [establishs] those who are stingy in renunciation, those deficient in virtue in that very virtue, the irascible in patience and gentleness, and the indolent in the perfection of energy. (5.37)
With unwearied conduct and valor, he compassionately directs those whose minds are distracted toward meditative concentration and wisdom, which dispel those distractions. (5.38)
Therefore, like the suns with their rays, he illuminates the world with undecaying and radiant splendors that extend across an infinite range.
Then, [he sees] beings who have committed evil falling into the hells and other realms,
as well as gods whose merit and lifespan are exhausted, yet who imagine themselves to be eternal.
Beholding with her divine power of vision the world struck by those various specific sufferings and their causes, she looked upon it.
Intense compassion arises within him; through compassion, he does not become negligent.
Being vigilant regarding the welfare of others, he attains inconceivable power.
Then he beholds the Tathāgatas dwelling in other world-systems,
as well as the magnificent arrays of qualities of their Buddha-fields and the excellence of their Saṅghas.
And he beholds the glorious conduct of the bull-like Bodhisattvas— their pure range of conduct and behavior, which results in the welfare of all the world.
And there, his aspiration is fulfilled with ease,
both through the dedication of virtue for the sake of others and through the excellence of his ethical discipline itself.
With superhuman, divine hearing purified by its object,
he heard various voices, both high and low, as if they were close at hand even though they were far away.
Those who stood far from compassion addressed him with harsh and unpleasant words,
as if they were the very flames issuing forth from the fire of his inner, blazing anger.
Though accompanied by the songs of apsarases, burdened by the sound of ornaments, and filled with the blare of divine trumpets, they have but one flavor: destruction.
Seeing those blinded by passion— who, though appearing as friends, are actually enemies—
being served [by them], he feels compassion for them because of that deception.

Then, due to fear and the particularity of his suffering, he was as if struck in the heart by the cries of the hell-beings, which were uttered with indistinct words and syllables and filled with the sound of distress.
The Greatly Compassionate One exerts supreme vigor from the very marrow of his bones,
like a fine horse urged on by a sharp-pointed goad.
Then, he hears the inexhaustible teachings on the Dharma from the Victors dwelling in various worlds, which inspire all sentient beings with the longing for nirvāṇa.
Then, having discerned the underlying tendencies and dispositions within the minds of others,
he who possesses the means of knowledge plants ever-new sprouts of merit.
And having recollected his former abodes for thousands of millions of eons,
he beholds the merits of the worlds, as well as the strength and weakness of their faculties.
Then, by virtue of that basis, through his supernormal power, he manifests multiple bodies;
he proceeds with fruitful discourse, teaching according to the capacity of the recipients.

In some places, he possessed a body marked with the characteristics of a king of sages, which was clearly variegated with signs all over it and whose perfection of luster was never contradicted even by the brilliance of a thousand suns.
Producing a festival for the eyes of men and bestowing a special joy through his speech,
he brings forth the manifestation of nectar for the sake of the state of a Victor among those who have faith in the Victors.
In some places, through his supreme tranquility, his sage-like glory, and his exceedingly distinguished conduct,
he who bears the form of a disciple of the Sage practices discipline toward those whose minds are worthy of such discipline.
With his lotus-feet honored by the crest-jewels of the gods like Mahendra,
he was like Kubera in some places, and in others, he possessed a wondrous splendor like that of Brahmā.
In one place his three eyes were wide open, adorned with a pure crescent moon upon his head;
in another, possessing the radiant splendor of the lord of the immortals, he bore the majesty of the king of serpents.
In some places his fingers were tawny like the fire of a thunderbolt, like the king of the Guhyaka kings;
in other places he possessed the marks of an immeasurable Conqueror, like the moon-like Sage with rays of virtue.
With the radiance of his vast chest shining with the rays of the brilliant Kaustubha gem,
he sometimes possessed the majesty of the king Garuḍa-bannered Viṣṇu, and at other times the splendor of Balarāma, the wielder of the plow.
In one place he possesses a white spear and inconceivable power; in another, he has the beautiful peacock as his vehicle;
in one place he is adorned by the mountains of sunrise and sunset; and in another, he possesses a form as pure as the moon and the sun.
In one place he bore the form of fire-gods, in another that of those who consume human offerings;
in some places he possessed the splendor of Varuṇa, and in others a body as beautiful as the god of love.
In one place, he—eager for the union of human love with the form of a beautiful woman—manifested the splendor of an ascetic; yet in another, his mind was detached from desire.
In some places, by assuming the roles of teacher, disciple, or king, he captivated the hearts of men;
and even in the hells, through his mastery over others' states of being, he brought about moments of liberation from suffering.
Then, through various kinds of activities and the extensive manifestations of the world's diverse inclinations,
he— continually endowed with the quality of compassion— brings about the welfare of the world here and there.
Having attained this vast excellence of distinction through reliance on the qualities of meditation,
one should strive for an even greater distinction, as if following unmistakable signs of hidden treasure.
If one’s stability in the wholesome is even weak, what loss is there for one accustomed to lax vows?
Therefore, one should strive for its increase; decline, however, results from the opposite.

Concentration is easily attained through effort, but its preservation is difficult, just as it is for one desiring victory who must immediately apply a remedy once the enemy has been conquered. (Ps 5.70)
Therefore, one should not trust in the extreme agility of the mind’s transformation,
just as one would not trust in having attained the immovable ground that is firm and free from fear or difficulty, were it not for the vast, unshakable earth.
For the detailed expansions of meditative concentration belonging to those who practice the conditioned path end in a fall;
therefore, one should rely on the cultivation of the supreme path by abandoning conceptual construction.
Having perceived that the conceptualization of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self is a deception arising from the fraud of conditioned phenomena,
one should not allow the mind to be occupied with the pursuit of such conceptualizations regarding existence.
Even when clear perception is possible, one still becomes a target for the arrows of the afflictions;
therefore, by completely pacifying that misfortune, one transcends the domain of Māra.
For the method of meditation does not become corrupted for the sake of purification by a fault in the physical seat;
rather, it is said that a seat accompanied by instability is "rough" (khaṭuṅka) precisely because of that.
It is said that this arises for the sake of establishing conventional practice;
for nothing whatsoever arises anywhere, because the logic of the possibility of existence and non-existence is untenable.
With a mind equal to space, he was then free from reliance even upon the three realms of existence;
his wise conduct was free from conceptual construction, and he shone effortlessly through his speech.
And he performs worldly activity that conforms solely to the welfare of the world;
yet, having attained mastery over the mind through the power of meditative concentration, he does not fall away from it.
Thereafter, he flourished through meditative absorptions (samādhis) dedicated to the welfare of others and accomplished according to the prescribed methods,
just as the ocean swells during the rainy season with the fresh waters brought by the rivers, his brides.
// A Summary of the Perfection of Meditative Concentration //
6. A Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom:
These merits, beginning with generosity, shine forth even more brilliantly when they have wisdom as their protector, like golden ornaments made radiant by the luster of inlaid jewels. (Ps_6.1)

For it is wisdom alone that bestows upon them the quality of efficacy in their actions, expanding it extensively—just as the mental continuum provides clarity to the sequence of the sense faculties when they are engaged in pursuing their own objects. (Ps 6.2)
Just as bodily machines, deprived of life and unfit for action, do not shine,
even so actions do not shine in the world when they are rendered inert by the loss of wisdom.
Among the faculties such as faith and the rest, wisdom is the leader, just as intellect is among the senses;
for one who has that as their companion discerns virtues and non-virtues, and thereby attains skill in the destruction of the afflictions.
For those who long for the fruit [of their actions], there is no purity of giving by its own nature due to the lack of wisdom;
for they say that giving for the sake of another is true generosity, whereas the rest is merely an application for the sake of increase, as it were.

But those Bodhisattvas whose eyes have been opened by wisdom, even after giving away their own flesh, neither undergo elation nor depression; they are like medicinal trees, free from conceptual construction.
Thus he attains the first stage, the foundation for the practice of supramundane goals;
free from anger, his mind overflowing with joy, his heart intent on the welfare of the world through great acts of giving.
Generally, upon that [ground] where one becomes a powerful universal monarch with an irreversible mind toward awakening,
and having been shown the true path by the qualities of wisdom, one then reaches the ground called Vimalā (The Stainless) through one's karma.
Having by his very nature become one of pure conduct and the lord of the four great continents,
his commands honored as the crest-jewel of kings, he attains the state of a Sun-like Arhat, just like the Lord of Sages.

Thereafter, among those deities who are subject to desire, and even in the world numbering two or three thousand [worlds], he attains sovereignty; and after that, having purified the stage of Prabhā, he becomes the lord of Prabhā.
How indeed can there be purity of virtue for one whose darkness has not been dispelled by wisdom?
For, generally, virtues are defiled by the faults of impatience due to separation from that [wisdom]. (Ps 6.11)
How could that wise person who possesses ethical discipline have any concern even for his own sake, let alone for the sake of others—
he who perceives the faults of the bonds of existence and desires to lift up all the worlds from them?
When the heart is stained by the adversaries of wisdom, how could the virtue of forbearance find stability?
For when a lord of the earth is timid-eyed in his failure to discern merit from demerit, he is no longer renowned for his virtues, like a hero [who has fled the field].
For those endowed with wisdom, the injuries inflicted by others become qualities of forbearance that produce steadfastness;
just as for noble elephants, the various types of goads applied to their trunks serve only to increase their specific excellences.
Even solitary vigor leads only to weariness; but for him who is supported by wisdom, the supreme quality of accomplishment arises in his task, which removes the exhaustion born of that effort.
Because there is nothing more subtle than this, it is the supreme pinnacle of skillfulness;
it never enters the path of the minds of those who are obscured by the defects of desire and the like.

How will their minds enter that meditative absorption, which is delightful through its exclusive bliss— minds that are gross due to the great accumulation of faults and have taken to a path of wisdom that is like a deviation from the right way?
For one whose mind lacks the exertion of wisdom, vision does not attain purity; without that, there is no ethical conduct.
Without that, right concentration is not attained; likewise, without it, the destruction of suffering cannot be achieved. (Ps 6.18)
But the wise person, perceiving fear in defects and seeing that happiness derived from qualities is bound up with suffering,
abandons the defects and proceeds by the path delightful with qualities, desiring the welfare of the world.
Exerting himself, he attains meditative concentration and achieves purity of speech, body, and mind;
thus, endowed with blameless power, he proceeds toward the arising of the world's welfare.
Through giving that fulfills even greater desires, through beloved and undepressed words like nectar,
and through a selfless and vigorous mode of conduct, he was equal toward all in his universal service for the sake of others.
Having demonstrated the universal [nature] within all phenomena and having won over their minds through love,
he— whose wheel of Dharma is unimpeded by the qualities of wisdom— establishes them in the bliss of nirvāṇa.

The affliction of fear, which takes refuge in the defects of lack of livelihood, miserable rebirth, death, and censure, cannot approach one who is presided over by these powers of wisdom and the rest. (Ps 6.23)
For all fears are born of the defilements, whereas wisdom does not dwell together with the defilements;
it is like the light of the sun, which has cleared away the clouds of autumn, cannot coexist with the spreading nets of darkness.
The power of the spreading radiance of wisdom renders those very darknesses that persist throughout the world— even at the rising of the thousand-rayed sun— nothing more than mere names.
There is nothing further to be done where that radiance attains its full power;
for when the world has been consumed by the fire at the end of the eon, no talk remains concerning what is yet to be burned.
All the luminaries combined together are not able to equal the radiance of wisdom;
therefore, there is no further increase beyond it, nor is there any possibility of its decline.
Training reaches fulfillment through ease for one who possesses ethical conduct and mental tranquility;
therefore, one devoted to wisdom should exert effort toward this with all one's might.

That investigation which, based on the truth, relies upon the manifestation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and is established through reasoning—this is, in brief, the entry into the objects of knowledge by those purified by wisdom throughout the three times. (Ps_6.29)
The portions of the conduct of the Sons of the Conquerors, purified by wisdom, spread their fame;
even those who are enemies of virtue and exceedingly deceitful have their hair stand on end through the power of wonder.
Even Māra, though possessed of an army, is not able to withstand the power of wisdom, whose radiance is most brilliant;
for the rays of wisdom cause his eyes to reel, so that he himself is unable to see.
Having spread the armor made of wisdom over the mind— which can withstand the fall of Kāmadeva’s arrows—
even a single person, remaining fearless, advances after having overcome the many forms and other objects arrayed before him.

Whether it be a lack of fortitude and self-discipline, or agitation caused by fear; whether it be the grief appropriate for the ignorant, or a deep-rooted passion of anger submerged within a small mind; or whether it be a state of dejection— (Ps 6.33)
In the wretched, there is the state of being stained by miserliness; in those possessed by passion, there is fickleness;
in those devoid of splendor, there is the quality of indolence; and in those who are arrogant, there is a nature lacking tranquility.

And those various subtle remnants of faults, though hidden within the caverns of their respective bases, wisdom utterly eradicates as soon as they arise, just as a solemn vow for the welfare of the world overcomes all obstacles.
Having fixed upon him the graceful splendor of his gaze— steadfast, gentle, and intent on the destruction of faults—
the Lord of Munis himself consecrates him with the exhilarating nectar of prophecy.

And when he shines upon his head, being consecrated by the rays from the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft of the Great Sages— rays that mock the splendor of the moon at midnight— he appears like the sacrificial fire of a ritual bathed with streams of clarified butter.
Since, having attained the status of crown prince among sages, his being has spread equally in all directions,
he pacifies the suffering of the world without effort, just as a great cloud raining down settles the dust.
All that radiance of the Sons of the Sugatas is brought forth by the power of wisdom;
what wonder is there in this, if such splendor should accrue even to a mother who is dear to her son? (Ps 6.39)
When even these ten qualities of the sages arise, it is solely by relying upon that [wisdom] that the excellence of power emerges,
as well as the entire remaining mass of jewels of qualities— uncommon, beautiful, and incalculable.
In this world, the treatises are like eyes; they are the repositories of specialized arts, various protective mantras, and the distinct, particular arrangements of the Dharma.
And whatever diverse paths of liberation they display for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world—all that is the manifestation of the power of their wisdom. (Ps 6.42)

For even in the state of a sovereign, Bodhisattvas do not undergo a transformation into an ugly nature despite sense objects that rival the divine; this is due to their being presided over by the minister of the quality of wisdom.
His loving-kindness has as its sole flavor the benefit of others and is entirely free from passion and attachment;
his supreme compassion for the sufferings of others has not fallen into the state of being weighed down by the burden of grief.
In the mind of sympathetic joy, there is freedom from agitation, and in equanimity, there is the absence of any engagement with darkness;
these various qualities shine forth even more intensely as the path that suppresses opposing factors through wisdom.

Who indeed in this world, seeking to accomplish the welfare of others, would destroy the darkness that is the sole cause of suffering, were it not for wisdom—that unimpeded radiance surpassing the sun—which dwells within the depths of the mind? (Ps 6.46)
To attain that, one should approach a venerable teacher who is capable of providing support, and collect this sacred learning— which is variegated with eighty types of divisions—
and having mastered it through the thirty-two [qualities], one should increase it by means of distinctions produced through right mental concentration.
One who has heard little is like a blind man; he does not know the path of meditative cultivation and, being devoid of it, does not contemplate.
Therefore, one should strive for learning, for wisdom arises from it as its basis through reflection and meditative cultivation. (Ps 6.48)

One should constantly strive for the increase of wisdom through questions, through specific discourses beginning with those on non-contention, through the investigation of the meaning of reality, and by one's own effort, as well as through meditation which increases those very qualities.
In brief, this is the method of wisdom and skillful means: meditative concentration focused on that goal, and the extensive study of the scriptures.
For from these two arises the source of all virtues, like the emergence of the light of wisdom from the fire-drills, as fire is produced from the two pieces of wood.
And by following the path practiced by wise men, one should avoid the dense thickets that cause delusion;
for obscured by them, one does not shine, even while standing at the peak of prosperity, like the moon hidden behind clouds clinging to the water.
Laziness, a mind prone to yawning, bad companionship, an addiction to sleep, and a disposition toward indecision;
a lack of curiosity regarding knowledge, like that of a sage, and questions constricted by false pride—these are the obstacles. (Ps 6.52)
Through wretchedness arising from self-mortification, there arises timidity regarding the approach of and respect for the learned;
there is also proficiency in false conceptualization and erroneous views which lead to delusion; but their opposites serve to pacify those [faults].

Skill in the aggregates, the sense-bases, and the elements, in the truths and the principles, in causes and their arising, and in the determination of purity and vehicles— this entire range of expertise regarding phenomena is the domain of the application of wisdom, which consists of eight types of conceptualization. (Ps 6.54)
Their form is indistinguishable from a mass of insubstantial foam; and the three types of sensation are like fragments of bubbles.
Even perception—like a mirage—deceives fools who are thirsty and scattered among the qualities of sensual desire, just as it lures deer.
The birth of conditioned phenomena is equal in quality to a plantain tree; even compared to an illusion, it is not more reasonable.
Depending upon it, the body—resembling a corpse overcome by the elements—wanders about, engaged in manifold conceptual constructions. (Ps 6.56)
There is no self here, nor does anything belonging to it exist; this is merely an aggregate, a collection of various impurities.
The notion of a "sentient being" deceives only the foolish, like a mechanical device well-constructed that moves according to its own will.
The self is not the eye, because it is subject to momentary destruction; likewise, it is not in the eye, nor is it there in the same way as the eye itself.
All the remaining internal sense-bases, without exception, are similarly devoid of the object of "mine" and are distinct from it.

Among the external elements, there is not even the slightest difference that contradicts their characteristics for those [elements] residing within the body. Furthermore, the consciousness-element is momentary; it is not the self, and therefore it is also equal to a flower in the sky.

Thus, this suffering arises solely for one whose mind is deluded by craving; but from the abandonment of that craving, supreme peace comes to be. The path that removes thirst consists of ethical conduct, vision purified through meditative concentration, and right view.
Seeing that things arise in dependence upon this or that, one whose vision is purified does not at all fall into the notions of "it exists" or "it does not exist.
To him, this world appears as consisting of illusion; therefore, he remains steadfast and unchanging in his mind regarding pleasure and the like.
Whatever has been and whatever will be is exactly like this; how could there be any possibility that suffering does not arise from these states of existence?
Thus, one who is free from passion does not rejoice even in past objects, nor does he delight in those yet to come.

What man, indeed, would feel passion for one whose harshness is evident in the diversity of his gestures, marked by hidden claws and glaring eyes, and who acts with the deceitful conduct of a servant? One should instead maintain trust toward him only as is appropriate after reflecting upon these deceptive behaviors.

Thus, even one whose mind is liberated, being compassionate and beholding the world destitute and amidst the interval of afflictions, possesses no inclination toward the lowly; due to his noble nature, he does not desire to enter nirvāṇa without having attained the qualities of a Buddha.

Having long ago set aside the two vehicles, which are incapable of accomplishing the welfare of the world, that King of Sages, who taught the path out of compassion, took his stand upon the Great Vehicle, whose very nature is the singular essence of benefiting others.
A noble mind does not incline toward that which is base and unworthy, nor does a lowly mind ever abide in the great;
a pure nature flows only with the pure. Likewise, this eternal principle applies to all other things as well.

Having reckoned pleasures and pains to be like dreams, and seeing that people are wretched due to the fault of delusion regarding them, how could you— casting aside the burden of activity that is delightful for the sake of others— allow yourself to be weighed down by the importance of your own self-interest?
He whose every action is for the sake of the welfare of the entire world, who has abandoned the sphere of the view of self and false conceit,
whose mind is everywhere peaceful, and who walks the path of non-duality— he is truly marvelous, being at peace through his conduct in this world.
This supreme vehicle brings about the purification of wisdom, for it is from its arising that the omniscience of the Great Sages emerges;
it proceeds as if becoming the very eyes of the world, like a radiance rising from the surface of the orb of the blazing sun.
Though he is crushed by the weight of the defects of saṃsāra, he is not worn out by the discernment of wisdom;
he does not fall into a state of despondency or exhaustion regarding his own self, as he generates the qualities of a Buddha in the world.

Beholding the wondrous power of the Sugata, with every part of their bodies covered in horripilation, they avoid the path leading to him; what indeed could be the cause for this, were it not for deceitful behavior?

Who indeed, unless their mind is overwhelmed by the age of Māra and Kali, or unless they harbor enmity toward this world, would dare to revile the vehicle of the Omniscient One—which is a treasury of the jewels of the qualities of the Perfectly Awakened Dharma and a way out from the mire of misfortune? (Ps 6.72)

In this lineage of the Kings of Jinas, who are intent on accomplishing the welfare of the world, when those whose vision is closed by ignorance stumble, whose mind would not be softened by compassion, and who would not exert firm vigor to pacify the fault of their delusion? (Ps 6.73)
For one who produces supreme purity through wisdom, how could liberation be far away? There is no other virtue higher than this; therefore, those who desire liberation should indeed cultivate it.
And this is the *Prajñāpāramitāsaṃgraha*, the compendium of the perfections.

Having properly gathered the potent honey from the lotuses of the Sūtras, which sprang from the lake of the pure mind of the Lord of Sages, like a diligent bee, [I have composed] this *Pāramitāsamāsa*.
